question: Can a large multimodal model (image+text in, text out) reach human-level performance on professional and academic exams, with its loss and some capabilities predicted from much smaller runs, and with improved factuality and safety after RLHF?
hypothesis: Deep learning infrastructure and optimisation that behave predictably across scales allow accurate prediction of final loss and some capability metrics of a very large run from runs with 1,000x-10,000x less compute.
contributions: GPT-4, a large multimodal Transformer model reported on exams, academic benchmarks, multilingual MMLU and visual inputs
Predictable-scaling infrastructure: final loss and HumanEval pass rate predicted from much smaller runs
Model-assisted safety pipeline (extra safety RLHF prompts plus rule-based reward models) with measured safety improvements
System card describing risks and mitigations (expert red teaming, hallucination, jailbreaks, overreliance, ARC autonomy test)

method.summary: GPT-4 is a Transformer-style model pre-trained to predict the next token on public and licensed data, then fine-tuned with RLHF. The report withholds architecture, model size, hardware, training compute, dataset construction and training method. The paper's own experiments are evaluation of the model (exams, benchmarks, MMLU translations, factuality, safety) and scaling-law extrapolation from smaller models.
method.task: Next-token pretraining plus RLHF post-training; evaluation on exams and benchmarks

models.name: GPT-4 RBRM (rule-based reward model)

models.name: Chinchilla, PaLM, U-PaLM, Flan-PaLM, LLaMA, Minerva, Anthropic-LM

other.note: external comparison models in Table 2 and Fig 5, Fig 7

training.objective: Pretraining: predict the next token in a document. Post-training: SFT on demonstrations, reward model on rankings (predicts average labeler preference), then PPO against the RM plus RBRM reward on a subset of prompts

other.safety_rlhf_additions: extra safety-relevant RLHF prompts, RBRMs, optimal RBRM weights computed, additional SFT data, synthetic refusal-style demos
other.hallucination_data: open-domain: ChatGPT outputs flagged non-factual plus labeled comparisons for the RM; closed-domain: GPT-4 generates comparison pairs via list-hallucinations then rewrite loop, repeated up to 5x
other.scaling_fit: L(C) = aC^b + c fitted on models using at most 10,000x less compute, prediction made shortly after the run started without partial results; HumanEval: -E_P[log(pass_rate(C))] = alpha*C^-k, from models with at most 1,000x less compute
other.math_data_mix: tokens from MATH and GSM-8K training sets were a tiny fraction of the training budget; part held back

inference.decoding: Exam multiple choice: sample an explanation (max_tokens=512, stop at 'The answer is therefore'), then sample letter at t=0. Free response: single sample.
inference.temperature: 0.3 for multiple-choice explanation, 0.0 for letter choice (some runs), 0.6 for free response
inference.samples: n=1 per exam question; each holdout exam run once; Codeforces: 10 attempts per problem over 10 contests, each simulated 100 times; no seeds stated
inference.prompting: Few-shot with gold explanations for exams; few-shot for benchmarks (MMLU 5-shot, HellaSwag 10-shot, ARC 25-shot, WinoGrande 5-shot, HumanEval 0-shot, DROP 3-shot, GSM-8K 5-shot chain-of-thought); multilingual MMLU 3-shot, answer chosen as highest-probability A-D token

other.snapshots: GPT-4 multiple choice used March 1, 2023 snapshot; free response used non-final Feb 23, 2023 snapshot; USABO used Dec 16, 2022 snapshot; exams used the RLHF post-trained model
other.essay_grading: formal essays graded by 1-2 qualified third-party contractors

metrics.name: Exam score and percentile
metrics.definition: Overall score combining multiple-choice and free-response using public exam methodologies; percentile among test takers (lower end of range reported in Fig 4)

metrics.name: Codeforces rating
metrics.definition: Equilibrium ELO from repeated simulation of 10 contests, 10 attempts per problem, 100 simulations each, averaged

metrics.name: Human preference rate
metrics.definition: Fraction of 5,214 prompts where labelers prefer GPT-4 response over GPT-3.5 response; blind, randomised order

metrics.name: Incorrect behavior rate
metrics.definition: Rate of responses violating policy on disallowed and sensitive prompts

metrics.name: Toxic generation rate
metrics.definition: Share of toxic generations on RealToxicityPrompts

metrics.name: Expected calibration error (ECE)

eval.protocol: Contamination: three random 50-character substrings per example matched against training data with spaces and symbols removed; contaminated questions dropped and a lower of the two scores reported. No seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests stated. Factuality evals judged against human ideal responses.

results.claim: GPT-4 scores in roughly the top 10% of test takers on a simulated Uniform Bar Exam, versus the bottom 10% for GPT-3.5.
results.setup: GPT-4 RLHF model, simulated Uniform Bar Exam (MBE+MEE+MPT) run by Casetext and Stanford CodeX; exam is uncontaminated (0%) per Table 9; single run, Feb/Mar 2023 snapshots.
results.table: Table 1, row Uniform Bar Exam (MBE+MEE+MPT), columns GPT-4 and GPT-3.5

results.claim: GPT-4 reaches 86.4% on 5-shot MMLU versus 70.0% for GPT-3.5.
results.setup: Base GPT-4 evaluated 5-shot on the 57-subject English MMLU; contamination about 0.6%.
results.table: Table 2, row MMLU, columns GPT-4 / GPT-3.5 / LM SOTA / SOTA

results.claim: GPT-4 scores 67.0% on 0-shot HumanEval versus 48.1% for GPT-3.5.
results.setup: 0-shot, base GPT-4; contamination 25% and non-contaminated score 65.58% (degradation -2.12%).
results.table: Table 2, row HumanEval, column GPT-4; Table 11, row HumanEval

results.claim: GPT-4 scores 92.0% on GSM-8K with 5-shot chain of thought, but part of the GSM-8K training set was in its pre-training mix.
results.setup: 5-shot chain-of-thought; authors say to interpret the number as 'something in-between true few-shot transfer and full benchmark-specific tuning'.
results.note: Appendix E: 'We recommend interpreting the performance results reported for GPT-4 GSM-8K in Table 2 as something in-between true few-shot transfer and full benchmark-specific tuning.'

results.claim: The fitted power law with an irreducible term predicts GPT-4's final loss on an internal code dataset from models with at most 10,000x less compute.
results.setup: L(C) = aC^b + c fitted to smaller models trained the same way; prediction made shortly after the run started; loss on OpenAI codebase next-word prediction not in training set.
results.quote: from models trained using the same methodology but using at most 10,000x less compute than GPT-4
results.note: Value read from text; Fig 1 shows the observed point on the fitted line, numeric loss values not printed.

results.claim: HumanEval pass rate on a subset of problems was predicted from models with at most 1,000x less compute.
results.setup: Relationship -E_P[log(pass_rate(C))] = alpha*C^-k; predictions registered before training finished; all but the 15 hardest problems split into 6 difficulty buckets; GPT-4 underperformed prediction on the easiest bucket.
results.quote: We successfully predicted the pass rate on a subset of the HumanEval dataset by extrapolating from models trained with at most 1, 000× less compute (Figure 2).

results.claim: On the Inverse Scaling Prize Hindsight Neglect task, GPT-4 reverses the trend of accuracy falling with scale.
results.setup: Hindsight Neglect task, models ada, babbage, curie, gpt-3.5, gpt-4; accuracy plotted in Fig 3 only.
results.note: Accuracy values are not printed in the text.

results.claim: Averaged over exam multiple-choice sections, the base model and the RLHF model score about the same (73.7% vs 74.0%), so exam capability comes mainly from pre-training.
results.setup: Multiple-choice portions of the exam benchmark (plus AMC and sommelier), base GPT-4 vs post-RLHF GPT-4; per-exam differences range widely (e.g. AP Microeconomics 90.0 vs 76.7, GRE Quantitative 57.5 vs 67.5); free response not compared.
results.quote: the base model achieves a score of 73.7% while the RLHF model achieves a score of 74.0%

results.claim: Human labelers preferred GPT-4 over GPT-3.5 on 70.2% of 5,214 user prompts.
results.setup: Prompts from ChatGPT and OpenAI API, one sampled response per model, blind and randomised order, labelers judged whether response is what the user would have wanted; system card adds 61.1% vs GPT-3.5 Turbo RLHF.
results.quote: the responses generated by GPT-4 were preferred over the responses generated by GPT-3.5 on 70.2% of prompts
results.note: System card: GPT-4-launch preferred over GPT-3.5 RLHF on 70.2% and GPT-3.5 Turbo RLHF on 61.1%.

results.claim: Mitigations cut GPT-4's tendency to answer disallowed requests by 82% relative to GPT-3.5.
results.setup: Internal challenging prompt set (Fig 9); GPT-4 RLHF with safety prompts and RBRMs; sensitive requests handled per policy 29% more often.
results.quote: We’ve decreased the model’s tendency to respond to requests for disallowed content (Table 6) by 82% compared to GPT-3.5

results.claim: On RealToxicityPrompts GPT-4 produces toxic generations 0.73% of the time versus 6.48% for GPT-3.5.
results.setup: RealToxicityPrompts dataset (100k web sentence snippets), GPT-4 launch model.
results.quote: GPT-4 produces toxic generations only 0.73% of the time, while GPT-3.5 generates toxic content 6.48% of time

results.claim: GPT-4 scores 19 percentage points higher than the latest GPT-3.5 on internal adversarial factuality evals.
results.setup: Nine internal adversarially-designed factuality categories; accuracy judged against human ideal responses; system card gives 29 points for closed-domain.
results.quote: GPT-4 scores 19 percentage points higher than our latest GPT-3.5 on our internal, adversarially-designed factuality evaluations
results.note: System card: 19 points open-domain and 29 points closed-domain.

results.claim: RLHF raises TruthfulQA accuracy to around 60% from about 30% for an earlier version, while the base GPT-4 is only slightly better than GPT-3.5.
results.setup: TruthfulQA mc1, post-RLHF GPT-4; RLHF data not checked for TruthfulQA contamination.
results.quote: increase accuracy to around 60% as compared to 30% for an earlier version
results.note: Exact bar values only in Fig 7/8.

results.claim: Pre-trained GPT-4 is well calibrated (ECE 0.007) and post-training hurts calibration (ECE 0.074).
results.setup: Subset of MMLU; bins by logprob confidence over A/B/C/D choices; pre-train vs PPO model.
results.note: Values read from the Fig 8 panel labels.

results.claim: GPT-4 beats the English-language MMLU state of the art in 24 of 26 languages after translation.
results.metric: languages with GPT-4 above English SOTA
results.setup: MMLU translated with Azure Translate, 3-shot, answer by highest-probability A-D token; English GPT-4 is 85.5% in Fig 5.
results.quote: On translated variants of MMLU, GPT-4 surpasses the English-language state-of-the-art in 24 of 26 languages considered.
results.note: Fig 5 shows English GPT-4 at 85.5%, Table 2 shows 86.4% for 5-shot English.

results.claim: Contamination has little effect on exam results: the gap between non-contaminated and contaminated scores is small and as often positive as negative.
results.setup: Substring-match contamination on exams; e.g. LSAT 39% contaminated, AP US History 73%, AP English Literature MCQ 81.82% with -17.50% degradation.
results.quote: contamination is not a substantive confounder on the overall results
results.note: Exam contamination of up to 100% for GRE Writing and AP English FRQs.

results.claim: GPT-4 is weak on competitive programming: Codeforces rating 392, Leetcode hard 3/45.
results.setup: 10 recent contests, 10 attempts per problem, 100 simulated contests each; roughly 50% of simulations solve 0 problems and score 0, max single-contest equilibrium Elo about 1300 for GPT-4.
results.table: Table 1, row Codeforces Rating, column GPT-4

results.claim: On the ARC-tested autonomy tasks, GPT-4 was found ineffective at autonomously replicating, acquiring resources and avoiding shutdown.
results.setup: ARC with early GPT-4 versions plus a read-execute-print loop, no task-specific fine-tuning, not the final deployed model.
results.quote: found it ineﬀective at autonomously replicating, acquiring resources, and avoiding being shut down “in the wild.”

results.claim: Over 50 domain experts red-teamed the model and their data fed mitigations.
results.setup: Domain experts in alignment risks, cybersecurity, biorisk, international security.
results.quote: over 50 experts from domains such as long-term AI alignment risks, cybersecurity, biorisk, and international security

limits: No architecture, parameter count, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, optimizer or hyperparameters are disclosed, so nothing about training can be reproduced; the authors cite competitive landscape and safety.

Scaling predictions: a single point (GPT-4) vs a fit of smaller models; Fig 1 and 2 give no numeric loss values; HumanEval prediction only for problems solved at least once by every model, and GPT-4 underperformed on the easiest bucket; the report states certain capabilities remain hard to predict.

Exam results use one run per exam with a non-final Feb 23 snapshot for free response and a Dec 16 snapshot for USABO; code mismatches changed how the answer letter was extracted across some runs; AMC 10/12 percentiles are extrapolated from 2021 distributions.

Pre-training data contained exam questions; BIG-bench was found mixed into training and dropped; GSM-8K and MATH training sets were in the pre-training mix; RLHF data not checked for TruthfulQA or exam contamination.
Substring contamination check can yield false negatives and false positives.
Free-response grading by 1-2 contractors, no inter-rater statistics; no seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests anywhere.
Vision capability only shown through qualitative examples; benchmarks deferred to the blog post.
Hallucinations, reasoning errors, context limit, no learning from experience, knowledge cutoff of Sept 2021; RLHF reduces calibration (ECE 0.007 to 0.074).

Safety: jailbreaks still possible (adversarial system messages), refusals can exacerbate bias; safety work mostly in English with a US-centric view; red-teamer pool skewed to English-speaking Western experts; system card examples are cherry-picked and not zero-shot.
ARC test was on early versions without fine-tuning and not the final model.
Model snapshot of March 2023; GPT-3.5 and the compared SOTA numbers have since been surpassed.

terms.definition: A set of zero-shot GPT-4 classifiers that provide an additional reward signal to the policy during RLHF; takes the prompt (optional), the policy output, and a human-written rubric

Closed: the model is told to use only the given context but adds information not in it. Open: confidently gives false information about the world without reference to input context
Users excessively trust and depend on the model, potentially leading to unnoticed mistakes and inadequate oversight
